scenes.contextualRelevance: The interview with David McGuinty discusses important political topics such as drug policy, youth engagement, and mental health, which are relevant in contemporary political discourse.

narrativeProgression.description: David McGuinty discusses the need for open and honest conversations about drug policy.
The conversation shifts to youth involvement in politics and their understanding of the science behind drug policies.
David McGuinty highlights the lack of medicinal value for alcohol and tobacco compared to the one illegal substance, alluding to marijuana.
The focus turns to the 'propaganda war' surrounding marijuana legalization and the need for evidence-based debate.
The interviewer mentions the connection between the weekend's events and the topics of youth engagement and mental health.
David McGuinty explains the Liberal party's efforts to spark a national dialogue about mental health issues and their impact.
The interview discusses the positive shift in public perception and acceptance of open debates about mental health.
David McGuinty acknowledges the contributions of others in raising the profile of mental health issues.
David McGuinty recounts his personal experiences as a criminal lawyer and the link he observed between criminal activity and substance abuse/mental health issues.
The interviewer shifts to a lighter topic, asking about youth apathy and voting engagement.
David McGuinty expresses optimism about the high number of young people participating in the event, emphasizing the importance of passing the torch to future generations.
The interviewer ends with a lighthearted question about a hypothetical arm-wrestling match.

scenes.thematicElements: Drug policy reform: Emphasis on open dialogue and evidence-based decision-making. Youth engagement in politics: Importance of passing the torch to future generations. Mental health awareness: Breaking down stigma and promoting open discussion.

places in Canada that are having an adult conversation.
I haven't come to ground in terms of how we should deal with this.
I know that there are all kinds of valid points we made on all sides of this debate in this
argument.
I'm looking forward to seeing how this resolution goes.
And the youth are really inspired by those kinds of things because they actually do the
research that it takes to understand this science behind it.
There's no medicinal value for alcohol.
You know, there's no medicinal value for tobacco, but there is for the one that's illegal.
And so it's a hard thing for people to understand and we feel that there's been sort of a propaganda
war that has been lost by the anti-prohibition crowd.
One of the things that informs everything we're doing here this weekend is to reclaim
an open and an honest debate about issues.
It's evidence and science-based.
And the debate around the legalization of marijuana is one that I'm hoping that's happening
here now is one that is open and evidence-based.
And there are all kinds of folks using all kinds of evidence and information to hopefully
convince folks about one way or another.
And that's what I'm looking forward to seeing this afternoon.
And it actually also touches two subjects.
One is youth and they're involvement in politics.
And the other is mental health.
And I'm wondering are current systems in place just inefficient or is there just not
enough funding or is it both?
One of the reasons why we brought a mental health opposition day motion to the floor of
the House of Commons as a caucus this last fall was precisely because we wanted to give
some momentum to the debate around mental health issues.
Mental health issues have a profound impact not just on health of an individual but a family
of community.
It has a huge bearing in productivity in terms of our organizations, our businesses, our
NGOs, our schools, our faculties, whatever.
And so we have to be open now.
And there's another area where I think finally the question of mental health is coming out
of the woodwork so to speak and people are accepting of an open debate about this.
And I think Bob raised on a fabulous job.
He spearheaded this whole motion.
I think it was just magnanimous the way he did it.
And that's our job as parliamentarians.
Raise these issues, raise the profile.
Let people know it's okay.
I remember when I began my career as a lawyer as a young criminal lawyer in my article in
period here in Ottawa.
I remember my biggest discovery was the relationship between the clients I was asked to work with.
Their dependency on substances or mental health issues.
And I think a lot of criminologists will support those views.
We'll share that evidence.
And so we've got to be open.
That's the way to tackle these things.
I'll tell you one thing.
Building more jail isn't going to solve it.
And one more thing before you go.
Youth.
Is there a way to finally crack the armor of apathy and get them to vote in higher numbers?
As soon as the people here are under 25.
No other parties manage to pull that together in a national convention to my knowledge in
the last 30 years.
I think this is an incredible breakthrough for us.
And to be frank, and to be honest about it, I don't think we predicted this extent of
youth take up.
It's fabulous.
And it's exactly what we need.
Because look, you have to pass the baton from generation generations.
A lot of, we're standing on successive shoulders of successive generations of people who built
the country and contributed and served.
Not just in public life, but in all kinds of settings.
And it's really good.
It's really good to see people turning up.
And at the Red Dog Project, we always end the interview with something lighthearted.
So who would win an arm wrestle between you and Dalton?
